title: Prompting & system prompts
summary: Learn to write clear prompts and system prompts that steer a large language model toward reliable, well-shaped answers.
objectives: Explain the difference between a system prompt and a user message
Write a system prompt that sets role, rules, and output format
Structure user prompts with context, task, and constraints

resources.label: Anthropic Prompt Library — ready-made example prompts

body_markdown:
## What is a prompt?

A **prompt** is the text you send to a large language model to get a response. The quality of that response depends heavily on how you ask. As a maths graduate, think of it like specifying a problem precisely: the clearer the statement, the better the solution.

There are two kinds of instruction you give Claude:

- The **system prompt** — standing rules that set the model's role, tone, and output format for the whole conversation.
- The **user message** — the actual question or task for this turn.

## System prompts: setting the rules

The system prompt is where you tell the model *who it is* and *how to behave* across every turn. Put the role, the constraints, and the required output format here. It stays in effect even as the user messages change.

In the Anthropic Messages API the system prompt is a separate top-level parameter — it is not just another message in the list.

```python
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()

msg = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=1024,
    system="You are a concise maths tutor. Answer in at most three sentences.",
    messages=[
        {"role": "user", "content": "What is a derivative?"}
    ],
)
print(msg.content[0].text)
```

## Structuring the user message

A strong user prompt usually has three parts: **context** (background the model needs), **task** (what to do), and **constraints** (format, length, tone). Spelling these out removes guesswork.

Vague: *"Tell me about this data."*

Specific: *"Here is a CSV of monthly sales. Summarise the three biggest trends in bullet points, one sentence each."*

## Few-shot examples

Often the fastest way to get the behaviour you want is to *show* it. Giving the model two or three examples of input and the desired output is called **few-shot** (or multishot) prompting, and it steers the model far more reliably than description alone.

```python
system = (
    "Classify each review as POSITIVE or NEGATIVE.\n"
    "Review: 'Loved it, fast and clean.' -> POSITIVE\n"
    "Review: 'Slow and rude staff.' -> NEGATIVE"
)

msg = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=20,
    system=system,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Review: 'Average meal, nothing special.'"}],
)
print(msg.content[0].text)
```

## Asking for a parseable format

When the model's output feeds into your own code, ask for a structured format such as JSON so you can parse it reliably instead of guessing. Keep your API key in an environment variable (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`) and never hard-code it.

## Common mistakes

- Being **vague** — fix by stating task, context, and format.
- **Mixing rules into every user message** — put persistent rules in the system prompt instead.
- **No output format** — specify it when code will read the result.
- **Over-stuffing** — too many instructions compete; keep it focused.

## Your task

Write a system prompt and one user message that make Claude act as a friendly explainer of a topic from your degree, and return its answer as three short bullet points.

We'll cover prompts, system prompts, few-shot examples, and how to call the Claude Messages A P I from Python. By the end, you'll be able to steer the model with confidence.

bullets: A prompt is the text you send to the model.
Answer quality depends on how you ask.

There are two kinds of instruction you give: the system prompt, which sets the rules, and the user message, which carries the actual question.

slides.title: System prompt: the rules
bullets: Sets the model's role and tone.
slides.narration: The system prompt is where you tell the model who it is and how to behave. You set the role, the tone, the constraints, and the required output format. Crucially, it stays in effect across every turn of the conversation, even as the user's questions change. Think of it as the standing rules of engagement.

slides.title: System prompt in the API
bullets: Claude takes a top-level system parameter.
The messages list holds the conversation.
Keep your A P I key in an env var.
slides.code:
msg = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=1024,
    system="You are a concise maths tutor.",
    messages=[{"role": "user",
               "content": "What is a derivative?"}],
)
slides.narration: In the Anthropic Messages A P I, the system prompt is its own top-level parameter called system. It is not just another item in the messages list. The messages list holds the back-and-forth of user and assistant turns. Notice we never hard-code a key; the client reads it from the environment variable. Here we tell Claude it is a concise maths tutor, then ask a question.

slides.title: Structure the user message
slides.narration: A strong user message has three parts: context, the background the model needs; task, what you actually want done; and constraints, like the format, length, and tone. Compare a vague request such as tell me about this data with a specific one: here is a sales file, summarise the three biggest trends in one-sentence bullets. The specific version removes all the guesswork.

slides.title: Few-shot examples
bullets: Show the model what you want.
slides.code:
system = (
  "Classify each review as POSITIVE or NEGATIVE.\n"
  "'Loved it, fast and clean.' -> POSITIVE\n"
  "'Slow and rude staff.' -> NEGATIVE"
)
slides.narration: Often the quickest way to get the behaviour you want is to show it, not describe it. Giving the model two or three worked examples of input and the desired output is called few-shot, or multishot, prompting. Here we show two labelled reviews so the model learns the exact pattern. When we then send a new review, it follows the same shape and labels it for us.

slides.title: Ask for a parseable format
bullets: Specify JSON when code reads the output.
Avoids guessing where each value lives.
slides.narration: When the model's answer feeds into the rest of your program, ask it to reply in a structured format such as Jason. That way your code can parse the result reliably instead of guessing where each piece of information sits. Specifying the exact shape, here a sentiment and a confidence number, turns free text into clean, machine-readable data.

slides.title: Common mistakes
bullets: Putting rules in every user message.
slides.narration: Let's flag the mistakes that catch most people. One: being vague, which forces the model to guess your intent. Two: repeating rules in every user message instead of putting them once in the system prompt. Three: forgetting to ask for an output format when code will read the result. And four: over-stuffing the prompt so instructions compete. Keep it focused and specific.
